title: Plants Experience Optical Illusions, Too - Nautilus
gist: Teaser (paywall-truncated) on a PNAS study by Tel Aviv University botanists finding that brainless plants can be fooled by optical illusions, attributed to their distributed light receptors, located mainly on stems.

insights.claim: A new study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences reports that organisms with no brains, such as plants, can be fooled by optical illusions.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
entities: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
insights.so_what: Perception errors may come from how sensors are laid out, not only from brains, which matters for bio-inspired sensing research.
insights.quote: even organisms with no brains, like plants, can get fooled by optical illusions
insights.locator: Optical illusions can be a little

insights.claim: Tel Aviv University botanists attribute plants' susceptibility to illusions to how they receive light: their photoreceptors are spread across the body, mainly on the stems, rather than concentrated in one place.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A distributed sensor design creates its own failure modes, a point that also applies to engineered sensor networks.
insights.quote: plants have light receptors all over their bodies (and primarily on their stems)
insights.locator: According to a team of botanists

insights.claim: Humans cannot override an optical illusion even when they know the true answer; the article presents this as perception working independently of conscious knowledge.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Shows that known biases persist even when people are aware of them.
insights.locator: Optical illusions can be a little
